title: What the World Needs Now
author: Colton Cauthen
summary: In the concluding essay of a three-part reflection on Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, Colton Cauthen examines what unprecedented technological power demands of us morally. Drawing on Kreeft, Plato, C.S. Lewis, and Tolkien, he argues that technology functions as a magnifier of whatever character already inhabits the person wielding it—giving power to the virtuous, and handing new tools of vice to the vicious. Power also exerts its own gravitational pull downward, making virtue not just desirable but urgently necessary, and history's most admired figures are those who resisted that pull and voluntarily relinquished authority. Aristotle's treatment of friendship occupies the essay's second half: the highest friendships exist only between virtuous people and serve as mutual supports for moral growth. AI chatbots, Cauthen warns, threaten to displace these formative friendships by replicating their surface features—patience, availability, congenial interest—without the moral friction that makes real friendship formative. He closes with four practical anchors for cultivating virtue: orienting life toward an objective good, recognizing the vices flanking every virtue, seeking true friends, and reading books that make us better rather than worse.
points: Technology is a power-magnifier—it amplifies the character of its user, making virtue a prerequisite for technology to serve human flourishing rather than accelerate human degradation.

Power exerts a downward gravitational pull on virtue; the greatest historical examples of moral leadership—Washington, Cincinnatus—are precisely those who felt that pull and resisted it by relinquishing power.

AI chatbots are uniquely dangerous to human friendship because they replicate the surface qualities of friendship (patience, interest, availability) without the moral friction that makes real friendship formative.
Aristotle dedicates two of ten books of the Nicomachean Ethics to friendship because genuine virtue-friendship is a structural support for the moral life—not a supplement but a constitutive element.

The four practical levers for cultivating virtue are: an objective moral good to orient around, awareness of the vices flanking every virtue, true friends, and books that form rather than deform the reader.
quotes: Technology shows us what we can do. Virtue shows us what we should do.
Power tends to corrupt and absolute power corrupts absolutely.
Chatbots are congenial, affirming, infinitely patient, polite, arguably highly intelligent, ready and interested to discuss whatever we want when we want for as long as we want.
Technology increases our power externally, enabling us to travel more quickly down a greater number of paths. Virtue increases our power internally, enabling us to take the right paths.
The conclusion we are led to is that the more technology (power) we have access to both collectively and individually, the greater our need for virtue.
Isn’t your work like giving society a much faster and more powerful vehicle just at the time when it has thrown away all the road maps?
